claim: Cortical bone maturation requires a reduction in cortical porosity.
source: We show that cortical maturation requires a reduction in cortical porosity, and a transition from low to high density bone, which continues even after cortical shape is established.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing cortical porosity reduction in control mice between 12 and 16 weeks of age.

claim: Cortical bone maturation requires a transition from low to high density bone.
source: We show that cortical maturation requires a reduction in cortical porosity, and a transition from low to high density bone, which continues even after cortical shape is established.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by micro-CT data showing changes in bone density distribution over time.

claim: The transition from low to high density bone continues even after cortical shape is established.
source: We show that cortical maturation requires a reduction in cortical porosity, and a transition from low to high density bone, which continues even after cortical shape is established.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing changes in bone density between 12 and 15 weeks of age when femoral length had plateaued.

claim: Both reduction in cortical porosity and transition to high density bone were delayed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: Both processes were delayed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by micro-CT data comparing Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice to controls at multiple time points.

claim: SOCS3 inhibits signalling by leptin, G-CSF, and IL-6 family cytokines (gp130).
source: SOCS3 (suppressor of cytokine signalling 3) inhibits signalling by leptin, G-CSF, and IL-6 family cytokines (gp130).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about SOCS3 function.

claim: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone, STAT3 phosphorylation was prolonged in response to gp130-signalling cytokines.
source: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone, STAT3 phosphorylation was prolonged in response to gp130-signalling cytokines, but not G-CSF or leptin.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation in response to IL-11, LIF, and OSM.

claim: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone, STAT3 phosphorylation was not prolonged in response to G-CSF or leptin.
source: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone, STAT3 phosphorylation was prolonged in response to gp130-signalling cytokines, but not G-CSF or leptin.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing no STAT3 phosphorylation response to leptin or G-CSF.

claim: Deletion of gp130 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice suppressed STAT3 phosphorylation in osteocytes.
source: Deletion of gp130 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice suppressed STAT3 phosphorylation in osteocytes and osteoclastic resorption within cortical bone, leading to rescue of the corticalisation defect, and restoration of compromised bone strength.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing reduced phospho-STAT3 positive osteocytes in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.

claim: Deletion of gp130 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice suppressed osteoclastic resorption within cortical bone.
source: Deletion of gp130 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice suppressed STAT3 phosphorylation in osteocytes and osteoclastic resorption within cortical bone, leading to rescue of the corticalisation defect, and restoration of compromised bone strength.
evidence: This claim is supported by histomorphometry data showing reduced osteoclast numbers in cortical voids of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.

claim: Deletion of gp130 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice led to rescue of the corticalisation defect.
source: Deletion of gp130 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice suppressed STAT3 phosphorylation in osteocytes and osteoclastic resorption within cortical bone, leading to rescue of the corticalisation defect, and restoration of compromised bone strength.
evidence: This claim is supported by micro-CT data showing normalized cortical porosity and bone density distribution in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.

claim: Deletion of gp130 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice led to restoration of compromised bone strength.
source: Deletion of gp130 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice suppressed STAT3 phosphorylation in osteocytes and osteoclastic resorption within cortical bone, leading to rescue of the corticalisation defect, and restoration of compromised bone strength.
evidence: This claim is supported by three-point bending test data showing improved post-yield deformation in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.

claim: Cortical bone development includes both pore closure and accumulation of high density bone.
source: We conclude that cortical bone development includes both pore closure and accumulation of high density bone, and that these processes require suppression of gp130-STAT3 signalling in osteocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by micro-CT data showing both reduction in cortical porosity and increase in high density bone during cortical maturation.

claim: Cortical bone development requires suppression of gp130-STAT3 signalling in osteocytes.
source: We conclude that cortical bone development includes both pore closure and accumulation of high density bone, and that these processes require suppression of gp130-STAT3 signalling in osteocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the rescue of the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype by gp130 deletion.

claim: Thin bony trabeculae arise from the cartilaginous growth plate during longitudinal growth.
source: During longitudinal growth, thin bony trabeculae arise from the cartilaginous growth plate, and, at the periphery of the metaphysis, they coalesce to form the cortical shell (Enlow, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Enlow, 1962.

claim: At the periphery of the metaphysis, trabeculae coalesce to form the cortical shell.
source: During longitudinal growth, thin bony trabeculae arise from the cartilaginous growth plate, and, at the periphery of the metaphysis, they coalesce to form the cortical shell (Enlow, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Enlow, 1962.

claim: Woven bone that makes up the initial cortex is gradually replaced with a stronger layered (lamellar) structure.
source: As well as achieving the distinctive thickened cortical shape, the woven bone that makes up the initial cortex is gradually replaced with a stronger layered (lamellar) structure (Enlow, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Enlow, 1962.

claim: In rodent bone, woven bone is partially replaced by modelling drift during growth.
source: In rodent bone, the woven bone is partially replaced by modelling drift during growth: new lamellar bone is deposited asymmetrically on both inner (endocortical) and outer (periosteal) cortical surfaces, and woven endochondral bone remains in the centre of the cortex (Shipov et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shipov et al., 2013.

claim: New lamellar bone is deposited asymmetrically on both inner (endocortical) and outer (periosteal) cortical surfaces in rodent bone.
source: In rodent bone, the woven bone is partially replaced by modelling drift during growth: new lamellar bone is deposited asymmetrically on both inner (endocortical) and outer (periosteal) cortical surfaces, and woven endochondral bone remains in the centre of the cortex (Shipov et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shipov et al., 2013.

claim: Woven endochondral bone remains in the centre of the cortex in rodent bone.
source: In rodent bone, the woven bone is partially replaced by modelling drift during growth: new lamellar bone is deposited asymmetrically on both inner (endocortical) and outer (periosteal) cortical surfaces, and woven endochondral bone remains in the centre of the cortex (Shipov et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shipov et al., 2013.

claim: In larger mammalian bones, including human, lamellar bone is deposited on endocortical and periosteal surfaces.
source: In larger mammalian bones, including human, in addition to deposition of lamellar bone on endocortical and periosteal surfaces (Maggiano et al., 2015), the inner cortical bone is remodelled into lamellar Haversian systems surrounding intracortical blood vessels (Enlow, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maggiano et al., 2015.

claim: In larger mammalian bones, the inner cortical bone is remodelled into lamellar Haversian systems surrounding intracortical blood vessels.
source: In larger mammalian bones, including human, in addition to deposition of lamellar bone on endocortical and periosteal surfaces (Maggiano et al., 2015), the inner cortical bone is remodelled into lamellar Haversian systems surrounding intracortical blood vessels (Enlow, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Enlow, 1962.

claim: The cellular changes and molecular mechanisms that control the establishment of the initial compact cortical bone structure remain undefined.
source: The cellular changes and molecular mechanisms that control the establishment of the initial compact cortical bone structure remain undefined.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors.

claim: Corticalisation occurs during rapid longitudinal growth.
source: Since corticalisation occurs during rapid longitudinal growth, the process has been difficult to quantify.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about bone development.

claim: Measurement of a cortical region of interest in the developing cortex during bone lengthening is difficult because a fixed position on the bone cannot be reliably identified due to the non-linear pattern of growth.
source: Bone growth in length occurs at the growth plate, and measurement of a cortical region of interest in the developing cortex in animals and humans during bone lengthening is difficult because a fixed position on the bone cannot be reliably identified due to the non-linear pattern of growth.
evidence: This claim is based on methodological challenges in studying bone development.

claim: Differences in positioning of a region of interest by even 1 to 2 mm may alter the analysis of any structural changes in bone.
source: Differences in positioning of a region of interest by even 1 to 2 mm may alter the analysis of any structural changes in bone (Seeman and Ghasem-Zadeh, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Seeman and Ghasem-Zadeh, 2016.

claim: Multiple scans of children with developing bones would be required to measure the process of corticalisation in humans.
source: Adding to this challenge, multiple scans of children with developing bones would be required to measure the process of corticalisation in humans, which raises safety concerns about radiation exposure effects on growing bone (Williams and Davies, 2006; Brenner and Hall, 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on methodological considerations for human studies.

claim: Multiple scans of children raise safety concerns about radiation exposure effects on growing bone.
source: Adding to this challenge, multiple scans of children with developing bones would be required to measure the process of corticalisation in humans, which raises safety concerns about radiation exposure effects on growing bone (Williams and Davies, 2006; Brenner and Hall, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Williams and Davies, 2006 and Brenner and Hall, 2007.

claim: Peak bone mass achieved in early adulthood strongly predicts later fracture risk after skeletal structure begins to decline with age.
source: Peak bone mass achieved in early adulthood strongly predicts later fracture risk after skeletal structure begins to decline with age (Seeman, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Seeman, 2002.

claim: Healthy girls and pre- and postmenopausal women with thinner or fewer trabeculae exhibit lower cortical area and higher cortical porosity.
source: Abnormalities in trabecular formation from the growth plate influence the structure of bone and determines fragility and risk of fracture; healthy girls and pre- and postmenopausal women with thinner or fewer trabeculae exhibit lower cortical area and higher cortical porosity (Bala et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bala et al., 2015.

claim: Trabecularisation occurs on the endocortical surface of bone in older individuals, leading to high cortical porosity and increased skeletal fragility.
source: In older individuals, a reversal of this process (trabecularisation) also occurs on the endocortical surface of bone, leading to a high cortical porosity and increased skeletal fragility (Zebaze et al., 2010); individuals over the age of 65 lose up to 50% of cortical bone mass during this process (Riggs et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zebaze et al., 2010.

claim: Individuals over the age of 65 lose up to 50% of cortical bone mass during trabecularisation.
source: In older individuals, a reversal of this process (trabecularisation) also occurs on the endocortical surface of bone, leading to a high cortical porosity and increased skeletal fragility (Zebaze et al., 2010); individuals over the age of 65 lose up to 50% of cortical bone mass during this process (Riggs et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Riggs et al., 1981.

claim: Cortical mass and dimensions determine the strength of long bones.
source: Cortical mass and dimensions determine the strength of long bones (e.g. femur, radius, ulna) (Ammann and Rizzoli, 2003), and fractures in long bones account for 80% of all osteoporotic fractures (Zebaze et al., 2010; Clarke, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ammann and Rizzoli, 2003.

claim: Fractures in long bones account for 80% of all osteoporotic fractures.
source: Cortical mass and dimensions determine the strength of long bones (e.g. femur, radius, ulna) (Ammann and Rizzoli, 2003), and fractures in long bones account for 80% of all osteoporotic fractures (Zebaze et al., 2010; Clarke, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zebaze et al., 2010 and Clarke, 2008.

claim: Current treatments for osteoporosis are less effective at cortical sites.
source: However, current treatments for osteoporosis are less effective at cortical sites, even though they prevent fractures in vertebral bone that contains a high proportion of trabecular bone (Clarke, 2008; Lindsay et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clarke, 2008 and Lindsay et al., 1997.

claim: Current osteoporosis treatments prevent fractures in vertebral bone that contains a high proportion of trabecular bone.
source: However, current treatments for osteoporosis are less effective at cortical sites, even though they prevent fractures in vertebral bone that contains a high proportion of trabecular bone (Clarke, 2008; Lindsay et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clarke, 2008 and Lindsay et al., 1997.

claim: Cortical bone consolidation was delayed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice lacking SOCS3 in Dmp1Cre expressing cells (osteocytes and late osteoblasts), particularly females.
source: Cortical bone consolidation was delayed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice lacking suppressor of cytokine signalling 3 (SOCS3) in Dmp1Cre expressing cells (osteocytes and late osteoblasts), particularly females (Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claim: Deletion of SOCS3 in the osteo-chondral lineage delayed formation of dense cortical bone.
source: In addition, deletion of SOCS3 in the osteo-chondral lineage also delayed formation of dense cortical bone (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Inhibition of cytokine signalling in osteocytes by SOCS3 is needed for timely formation of cortical bone.
source: This indicates that inhibition of cytokine signalling in osteocytes by SOCS3 is needed for timely formation of cortical bone.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the delayed cortical bone formation in SOCS3-deficient mice.

claim: SOCS3 provides negative feedback for the leptin, G-CSF, and gp130 receptors.
source: However, SOCS3 provides negative feedback for a range of cytokine receptors, including the leptin, G-CSF, and gp130 receptors.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about SOCS3 function.

claim: The gp130 receptor is utilized by the IL-6 family of cytokines, which includes Interleukin 6 (IL-6), Interleukin 11 (IL-11), oncostatin M (OSM), cardiotrophin 1 (CT-1) and leukaemia inhibitory factor (LIF).
source: The latter is utilized by the IL-6 family of cytokines, which includes Interleukin 6 (IL-6), Interleukin 11 (IL-11), oncostatin M (OSM), cardiotrophin 1 (CT-1) and leukaemia inhibitory factor (LIF).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about cytokine receptor families.

claim: Leptin, G-CSF and IL-6 family cytokines all have the potential to modify cortical development since they each promote bone formation through local action in bone.
source: Leptin, G-CSF and IL-6 family cytokines all have the potential to modify cortical development since they each promote bone formation through local action in bone (McGregor et al., 2019; Sims et al., 2005; Walker et al., 2008; Cornish et al., 1993; Walker et al., 2010; Winkler et al., 2010; Scheller et al., 2010), modify gene expression by osteocytes (McGregor et al., 2019; Walker et al., 2010), and, in some cases, promote bone resorption (Tamura et al., 1993; Richards et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies showing effects of these cytokines on bone.

claim: Leptin, G-CSF and IL-6 family cytokines modify gene expression by osteocytes.
source: Leptin, G-CSF and IL-6 family cytokines all have the potential to modify cortical development since they each promote bone formation through local action in bone (McGregor et al., 2019; Sims et al., 2005; Walker et al., 2008; Cornish et al., 1993; Walker et al., 2010; Winkler et al., 2010; Scheller et al., 2010), modify gene expression by osteocytes (McGregor et al., 2019; Walker et al., 2010), and, in some cases, promote bone resorption (Tamura et al., 1993; Richards et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McGregor et al., 2019 and Walker et al., 2010.

claim: Some cytokines (leptin, G-CSF, IL-6 family) promote bone resorption.
source: Leptin, G-CSF and IL-6 family cytokines all have the potential to modify cortical development since they each promote bone formation through local action in bone (McGregor et al., 2019; Sims et al., 2005; Walker et al., 2008; Cornish et al., 1993; Walker et al., 2010; Winkler et al., 2010; Scheller et al., 2010), modify gene expression by osteocytes (McGregor et al., 2019; Walker et al., 2010), and, in some cases, promote bone resorption (Tamura et al., 1993; Richards et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tamura et al., 1993 and Richards et al., 2000.

claim: Phenotypes caused by SOCS3 deficiency in other organs were rescued by IL-6 deletion.
source: Although phenotypes caused by SOCS3 deficiency in other organs were rescued by IL-6 deletion (Croker et al., 2003), this was not the case in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Croker et al., 2003.

claim: The Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype was not rescued by IL-6 deletion.
source: Although phenotypes caused by SOCS3 deficiency in other organs were rescued by IL-6 deletion (Croker et al., 2003), this was not the case in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claim: There was no significant difference in femoral length between Dmp1Cre and Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice when scanned on a weekly basis.
source: There was no significant difference in femoral length between Dmp1Cre and Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice when scanned on a weekly basis (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A minor but statistically significant growth-related increase in femoral length was detected between 12 and 16 weeks in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, consistent with a plateau of longitudinal growth by this time point.
source: A minor but statistically significant growth-related increase in femoral length was detected between 12 and 16 weeks in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, consistent with a plateau of longitudinal growth by this time point (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: From 12 to 16 weeks of age, the high cortical porosity was significantly reduced in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, but did not reach the low normal levels seen in control (Dmp1Cre) mice.
source: From 12 to 16 weeks of age, as expected, the high cortical porosity was significantly reduced in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, but did not reach the low normal levels seen in control (Dmp1Cre) mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cortical porosity was elevated in the diaphysis of 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: Even though the more mature diaphysis has a lower cortical porosity than the metaphysis, cortical porosity was also elevated in the diaphysis of 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Control mice already have consolidated cortical bone in the metaphysis by 12 weeks of age.
source: These indicated that, while control mice already have consolidated cortical bone in the metaphysis by 12 weeks of age, this structure was not fully formed even by 16 weeks of age in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
evidence: This claim is based on visual analysis of micro-CT videos and images.

claim: Cortical bone structure was not fully formed even by 16 weeks of age in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: These indicated that, while control mice already have consolidated cortical bone in the metaphysis by 12 weeks of age, this structure was not fully formed even by 16 weeks of age in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
evidence: This claim is based on visual analysis of micro-CT videos and images.

claim: In control mice, although the cortical shape was already formed, and cortical porosity did not reduce between 12 and 16 weeks, there was an increase in bone material density.
source: In control mice, although the cortical shape was already formed, and cortical porosity did not reduce in this time period (Figure 1C), there was an increase in bone material density (shift in colour from blue to white, Video 1; Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudocolorized micro-CT images and videos showing density changes.

claim: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, cortical holes were filled between 12 and 16 weeks of age.
source: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, not only were cortical holes filled, consistent with quantitation in Figure 1C, but trabecular bone was remodelled into fewer elements, and some regions of bone in the cortex became more dense (shifting from yellow to blue to white in the pseudocolourised images) (Video 2; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudocolorized micro-CT images and videos.

claim: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, trabecular bone was remodelled into fewer elements between 12 and 16 weeks of age.
source: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, not only were cortical holes filled, consistent with quantitation in Figure 1C, but trabecular bone was remodelled into fewer elements, and some regions of bone in the cortex became more dense (shifting from yellow to blue to white in the pseudocolourised images) (Video 2; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudocolorized micro-CT images and videos.

claim: Some regions of bone in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortex became more dense between 12 and 16 weeks of age.
source: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, not only were cortical holes filled, consistent with quantitation in Figure 1C, but trabecular bone was remodelled into fewer elements, and some regions of bone in the cortex became more dense (shifting from yellow to blue to white in the pseudocolourised images) (Video 2; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudocolorized micro-CT images and videos.

claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice do not exhibit clearly distinguishable trabecular and cortical bone in the metaphysis at 12–15 weeks of age.
source: However Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice do not exhibit clearly distinguishable trabecular and cortical bone in the metaphysis at 12–15 weeks of age (Cho et al., 2017); instead they form a foamy network similar to that previously described during much earlier stages of cortical bone development (i.e. between birth and 14 days of age in C57BL/6 mice (Bortel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cho et al., 2017 and Bortel et al., 2015.

claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice form a foamy network similar to that described during much earlier stages of cortical bone development (between birth and 14 days of age in C57BL/6 mice).
source: However Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice do not exhibit clearly distinguishable trabecular and cortical bone in the metaphysis at 12–15 weeks of age (Cho et al., 2017); instead they form a foamy network similar to that previously described during much earlier stages of cortical bone development (i.e. between birth and 14 days of age in C57BL/6 mice (Bortel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bortel et al., 2015.

claim: In Dmp1Cre mice, very little high density bone was detected in the metaphysis at 12 weeks of age.
source: In Dmp1Cre mice, very little high density bone was detected in the metaphysis at 12 weeks of age (Figure 2B), consistent with the (non-calibrated) pseudocolourised images (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Dmp1Cre mice, by 15 weeks of age, total bone volume (as a proportion of metaphyseal volume) was significantly increased compared to 12 weeks.
source: In the same animals, by 15 weeks of age, total bone volume (as a proportion of metaphyseal volume) was significantly increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Dmp1Cre mice between 12 and 15 weeks, the high density bone proportion increased approximately 14 fold.
source: There were significant changes in all three densities of bone over the three week time period: the high density proportion increased approximately 14 fold, while the mid- and low- density bone were both significantly reduced by approximately 12% and 30%, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Dmp1Cre mice between 12 and 15 weeks, mid-density bone was significantly reduced by approximately 12%.
source: There were significant changes in all three densities of bone over the three week time period: the high density proportion increased approximately 14 fold, while the mid- and low- density bone were both significantly reduced by approximately 12% and 30%, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Dmp1Cre mice between 12 and 15 weeks, low-density bone was significantly reduced by approximately 30%.
source: There were significant changes in all three densities of bone over the three week time period: the high density proportion increased approximately 14 fold, while the mid- and low- density bone were both significantly reduced by approximately 12% and 30%, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice had more bone within the metaphysis (higher total bone volume/cross sectional area) than Dmp1Cre mice at both 12 and 15 weeks of age.
source: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice had more bone within the metaphysis (higher total bone volume/cross sectional area) than Dmp1Cre mice at both 12 and 15 weeks of age (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At 12 weeks, Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice had a two-fold greater proportion of low density bone compared to Dmp1Cre mice.
source: At 12 weeks, this was due to a two-fold greater proportion of low density bone.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: As Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice aged from 12 to 15 weeks, total bone volume did not change, but the proportion of low density bone decreased, while the proportion of high density bone increased.
source: As Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice aged, total bone volume did not change, but the proportion of low density bone decreased, while the proportion of high density bone increased (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In both Dmp1Cre and Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, as the metaphysis ages, low density bone is replaced with higher density bone.
source: This indicates that in both Dmp1Cre and Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, as the metaphysis ages, low density bone is replaced with higher density bone.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing changes in bone density distribution over time.

claim: The metaphyseal region as a whole contains both immature and mature cortical bone, with the most mature bone at greatest distance from the growth plate.
source: Since new bone forms at the growth plate, we reasoned that the metaphyseal region as a whole would contain both immature and mature cortical bone, with the most mature bone at greatest distance from the growth plate (Rauch, 2012), and that this could be measured to identify differences in the corticalisation process between Dmp1Cre and Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
evidence: This claim is based on reasoning supported by a citation to Rauch, 2012.

claim: At 12 weeks of age, Dmp1Cre mice exhibited a ~2.5 fold increase in mid-density bone at the proximal compared to the distal end of the metaphysis.
source: At 12 weeks of age, Dmp1Cre mice exhibited a ~2.5 fold increase in mid-density bone (Figure 3B) at the proximal compared to the distal end (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 12 weeks of age in Dmp1Cre mice, there was very little high density bone present, but there was a significantly greater proportion in the last slice compared to the first 8 slices (~10 fold greater).
source: Although there was very little high density bone present at 12 weeks of age, there was a significantly greater proportion in the last slice compared to the first 8 slices (~10 fold greater, p=0.037).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Metaphyseal bone in the 12 week old murine femur transitions from mainly low density, to mainly mid-density bone with increasing distance from the growth plate.
source: Metaphyseal bone in the 12 week old murine femur therefore transitions from mainly low density, to mainly mid-density bone with increasing distance from the growth plate.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the slice-by-slice analysis data.

claim: When Dmp1Cre control mice were assessed at 15 weeks of age along the metaphysis, the control bones exhibited an approximately 4-fold increase in the proportion of high density bone from the distal to the proximal end of the metaphysis.
source: When Dmp1Cre control mice were assessed at 15 weeks of age along the metaphysis, the control bones exhibited an approximately 4-fold increase in the proportion of high density bone from the distal to the proximal end or the metaphysis, such that high density bone was the dominant type of bone present at the proximal end Figure 3C.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At 15 weeks of age in Dmp1Cre mice, high density bone was the dominant type of bone present at the proximal end of the metaphysis.
source: When Dmp1Cre control mice were assessed at 15 weeks of age along the metaphysis, the control bones exhibited an approximately 4-fold increase in the proportion of high density bone from the distal to the proximal end or the metaphysis, such that high density bone was the dominant type of bone present at the proximal end Figure 3C.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The transition from low to high density cortical bone that occurs as bone matures between 12 to 15 weeks can be assessed at a single time point by a slice-by-slice analysis of the metaphysis.
source: This shows that the transition from low to high density cortical bone that occurs as bone matures between 12 to 15 weeks can also be assessed at a single time point by a slice-by-slice analysis of the metaphysis, and that bone tissue matures even after cortical consolidation has occurred.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the slice-by-slice analysis data.

claim: Bone tissue matures even after cortical consolidation has occurred.
source: This shows that the transition from low to high density cortical bone that occurs as bone matures between 12 to 15 weeks can also be assessed at a single time point by a slice-by-slice analysis of the metaphysis, and that bone tissue matures even after cortical consolidation has occurred.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing continued density changes after cortical shape is established.

claim: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice at 12 weeks of age the shape of the density curve was distinctly different to that of age-matched Dmp1Cre mice.
source: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice at 12 weeks of age the shape of the density curve was distinctly different to that of age-matched Dmp1Cre mice (compare Figure 3D to Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 3D and 3B.

claim: Low density bone was doubled in the proximal region of 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre mice.
source: This was most notable in low density bone which was doubled in the proximal region compared to Dmp1Cre mice; this was statistically significant (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 shows comparisons between genotypes at each slice and bone density level).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, the proportion of low density bone reduced significantly with distance from the growth plate, as mid-density bone increased.
source: The proportion of low density bone reduced significantly with distance from the growth plate, as mid-density bone increased (distance effect, p<0.0001 for both).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, there was no significant change in the very low proportion of high density bone, which was absent in most samples even in the proximal slices.
source: There was no significant change in the very low proportion of high density bone, which was absent in most samples even in the proximal slices.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora accumulate mid-density bone in regions furthest from the growth plate in the same manner as the control mice, but it is on the background of a high level of immature low density bone.
source: Their femora accumulate mid-density bone in regions furthest from the growth plate in the same manner as the control mice, but it is on the background of a high level of immature low density bone.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the slice-by-slice analysis data.

claim: At 15 weeks of age the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora had more high density bone in regions furthest from the growth plate.
source: At 15 weeks of age the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora, like the Dmp1Cre femora, had more high density bone in regions furthest from the growth plate (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Although Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora started with a lower level of high density bone than controls at 15 weeks, they reached the same level of high density bone.
source: Although Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora started with a lower level of high density bone than controls, they reached the same level of high density bone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora at 15 weeks of age had more low density bone than age-matched controls in the region closest to the growth plate.
source: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora at 15 weeks of age also had more low density bone than age-matched controls in the region closest to the growth plate, as at 12 weeks (Figure 3—figure supplement 2); and unlike age-matched Dmp1Cre controls, this declined significantly along the length of the bone.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In 15 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora, low density bone declined significantly along the length of the bone, unlike age-matched Dmp1Cre controls.
source: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora at 15 weeks of age also had more low density bone than age-matched controls in the region closest to the growth plate, as at 12 weeks (Figure 3—figure supplement 2); and unlike age-matched Dmp1Cre controls, this declined significantly along the length of the bone.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora at 15 weeks had a higher proportion of mid-density bone compared to controls along almost the full length of the metaphysis.
source: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora also had a higher proportion of mid-density bone compared to controls along almost the full length of the metaphysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora exhibit both the reduction in cortical porosity and the increase in bone density associated with corticalisation, but this process occurs in the presence of a greater quantity of low density bone than in control mice of the same age and sex.
source: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora therefore exhibit both the reduction in cortical porosity and the increase in bone density associated with corticalisation. However, this process occurs in the presence of a greater quantity of low density bone than in control mice of the same age and sex.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing changes in cortical porosity and bone density distribution.

claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice have immature cortical bone compared with their age-matched controls.
source: This confirms that Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice have immature cortical bone compared with their age-matched controls.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing differences in bone density distribution and histological appearance.

claim: At 16 weeks old, in approximately 40% of the bone closest to the endocortical edge, control bone exhibited mature lamellar bone, characterised by flattened and aligned osteocytes with dendritic processes primarily running perpendicular to the endocortical surface.
source: At this site, in approximately 40% of the bone closest to the endocortical edge, control bone exhibited mature lamellar bone, characterised by flattened and aligned osteocytes with dendritic processes primarily running perpendicular to the endocortical surface (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ploton silver staining shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Osteocytes in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone at 16 weeks old were more rounded, showed no ordered orientation, and the bone contained many cement lines.
source: In contrast, osteocytes in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone at the same anatomical location were more rounded, showed no ordered orientation, and the bone contained many cement lines (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ploton silver staining shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The newly forming Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone does not contain cartilage remnants.
source: Since we have previously reported that the newly forming Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone does not contain cartilage remnants (Cho et al., 2017), the abundant cement lines of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone do not reflect retention of immature endochondral cartilage and woven bone.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claim: The abundant cement lines of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone reflect rapid remodelling and replacement of that structure with woven bone.
source: Since we have previously reported that the newly forming Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone does not contain cartilage remnants (Cho et al., 2017), the abundant cement lines of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone do not reflect retention of immature endochondral cartilage and woven bone. Rather, it reflects rapid remodelling and replacement of that structure with woven bone.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the histological observations and previous findings.

claim: Although the control cortical bone had accrued lamellar bone at 16 weeks, this has not occurred in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortex.
source: Although the control cortical bone had accrued lamellar bone at this time point, this has not occurred in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: Female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora at 26 weeks had normal bone mass but significantly less high- and mid- density bone, and more low-density bone than controls.
source: Using our three-tiered density analysis, we observed that although female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora had normal bone mass, they still had significantly less high- and mid- density bone, and more low-density bone than controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice showed prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation in response to all IL-6 family cytokines tested (IL-11, LIF and OSM) compared to Dmp1Cre mice.
source: When tested in a calvarial injection model, Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice showed prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation in response to all IL-6 family cytokines tested (IL-11, LIF and OSM) compared to Dmp1Cre mice (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4.

claim: There was no STAT3 phosphorylation response to either Leptin or G-CSF in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: In contrast, there was no STAT3 phosphorylation response to either Leptin or G-CSF (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data not shown in the manuscript.

claim: The Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype may result from prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation downstream of gp130 binding cytokines, including IL-11, LIF and OSM.
source: The Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype may therefore result from prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation downstream of gp130 binding cytokines, including IL-11, LIF and OSM.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the STAT3 phosphorylation data.

claim: There was no difference in basal phospho-STAT3 levels detected by western blot between Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f and control mice.
source: There was no difference in basal phospho-STAT3 levels detected by western blot, consistent with observations in other cell-specific knockouts of SOCS3 (Croker et al., 2003; Croker et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data and citations to Croker et al., 2003 and 2004.

claim: The lack of difference in basal phospho-STAT3 levels is likely due to the low level of STAT3 phosphorylation in basal conditions relative to the stimulated response, or may reflect that the tissue contains a mixture of cell types, including cells with normal levels of SOCS3.
source: This is likely due to the low level of STAT3 phosphorylation in basal conditions relative to the stimulated response, or may reflect that the tissue contains a mixture of cell types, including cells with normal levels of SOCS3.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the reasons for the lack of difference in basal phospho-STAT3 levels.

claim: STAT3 phosphorylation was elevated in osteocytes in both male and female tibial samples from Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: STAT3 phosphorylation was elevated in osteocytes by immunohistochemical quantitation of phospho-STAT3 positive osteocytes, which were significantly elevated in both male and female tibial samples (Figure 4D), confirming that a lack of SOCS3 negative feedback results in elevated STAT3 signalling in response to endogenous stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A lack of SOCS3 negative feedback results in elevated STAT3 signalling in response to endogenous stimuli.
source: STAT3 phosphorylation was elevated in osteocytes by immunohistochemical quantitation of phospho-STAT3 positive osteocytes, which were significantly elevated in both male and female tibial samples (Figure 4D), confirming that a lack of SOCS3 negative feedback results in elevated STAT3 signalling in response to endogenous stimuli.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype is not rescued by IL-6 deletion.
source: We previously reported that the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype is not rescued by IL-6 deletion (Cho et al., 2017), and since all other gp130-binding cytokines tested induced prolonged phosphorylation, we next determined whether gp130 deletion in osteocytes might resolve the phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claim: The previously published gp130-flox mouse is reported to increase release of soluble gp130 by targeted cells.
source: The rationale for this was that the gp130-flox mouse we previously utilised (Standal et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2014) is reported to increase release of soluble gp130 by targeted cells (Betz et al., 1998), which might act locally as an inhibitor of signalling in other cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Standal et al., 2014, Johnson et al., 2014, and Betz et al., 1998.

claim: The new mouse with Dmp1Cre targeted deletion (Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f) showed reduced Il6st transcription in bone.
source: The new mouse with Dmp1Cre targeted deletion (Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f) showed reduced Il6st transcription in bone (Table 1) and exhibited a similar phenotype to that observed with the previously published gp130 targeting strategy (Dmp1Cre:gp130f/f).
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA data shown in Table 1.

claim: The Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f mouse exhibited low trabecular bone mass, increased periosteal circumference, and reduced bone formation with no reduction in bone resorption.
source: The new mouse with Dmp1Cre targeted deletion (Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f) showed reduced Il6st transcription in bone (Table 1) and exhibited a similar phenotype to that observed with the previously published gp130 targeting strategy (Dmp1Cre:gp130f/f). That is, the mouse exhibited low trabecular bone mass, increased periosteal circumference, and reduced bone formation with no reduction in bone resorption (Table 1; Standal et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1 and citations to Standal et al., 2014 and Johnson et al., 2014.

claim: gp130 in osteocytes is required for normal bone formation and normal trabecular bone mass.
source: This confirmed our earlier finding that gp130 in osteocytes is required for normal bone formation and normal trabecular bone mass.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f phenotype and previous findings.

claim: Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f mice had normal cortical porosity.
source: When Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f mice, which themselves had normal cortical porosity (Figure 5A) were crossed with Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, the resulting Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited normalised cortical porosity at 12 weeks of age in both male and female mice (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited normalised cortical porosity at 12 weeks of age in both male and female mice.
source: When Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f mice, which themselves had normal cortical porosity (Figure 5A) were crossed with Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, the resulting Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited normalised cortical porosity at 12 weeks of age in both male and female mice (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Levels of low- and mid-density bone were each significantly reduced in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared with the high levels observed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice in both males and females.
source: Normalisation was also observed in bone volume segregated by density. Levels of low- and mid-density bone were each significantly reduced in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared with the high levels observed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice; this was observed in both males and females (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice showed a density pattern very similar to wild type mice of the same age.
source: When the density profiles were assessed along the length of the bone, female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice showed a pattern that was very similar to wild type mice of the same age (compare Figure 5E to Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 5E and 3A.

claim: The high volume of low-density bone seen in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice at the distal end was not observed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.
source: The high volume of low-density bone seen in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice at the distal end (Figure 5E) was not observed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: The proportion of low density bone was significantly lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice in the distal region.
source: When compared directly (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) the proportion of low density bone was significantly lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice in this region.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The level of mid-density bone was significantly lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: The level of mid-density bone was also significantly lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating a return to a phenotype similar to control mice (compare with Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The proportion of high density bone increased in both Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f and Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f female femora.
source: The proportion of high density bone increased in both Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f and Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f female femora (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: Deletion of gp130 from osteocytes normalises the delayed corticalisation of female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: These results indicate that deletion of gp130 from osteocytes normalises the delayed corticalisation of female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing normalized cortical porosity and bone density distribution in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.

claim: Male Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice exhibited a lesser delay in corticalisation compared to females.
source: Male Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice exhibited a lesser delay in corticalisation compared to females in our earlier study (Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claim: Male Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited the same differences compared to sex-matched Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice as seen in the females: a lower level of low density and mid-density bone, and no difference in high density bone.
source: When gp130 was deleted from osteocytes, the male Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited the same differences compared to sex-matched Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice as seen in the females: a lower level of low density and mid-density bone, and no difference in high density bone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Cortical consolidation specifically requires SOCS3 mediated suppression of IL-6 family cytokine signalling within osteocytes in both male and female mice.
source: This indicates that cortical consolidation specifically requires SOCS3 mediated suppression of IL-6 family cytokine signalling within osteocytes in both male and female mice.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the rescue of the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype by gp130 deletion in both sexes.

claim: There was no clear reduction in calcein labels in the metaphyseal cortex in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: There was no clear reduction in calcein labels in the metaphyseal cortex in Dmp1Cre: Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: More cortical pores (containing blood vessels and sometimes bone marrow) were seen in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.
source: Extensive double-labelled surfaces were observed in both genotypes in this region, but more cortical pores (containing blood vessels and sometimes bone marrow) were seen in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: The pore area was reduced in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f bone by approximately 60% compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone.
source: When quantified, the pore area was reduced in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f bone by approximately 60% (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histomorphometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both osteoclasts and osteoblasts were detected within the pores in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone.
source: Both osteoclasts and osteoblasts were detected within the pores in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone, and due to the reduction in pore area, the number of osteoclasts and osteoblasts were lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f bone than Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by histomorphometry data shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: Due to the reduction in pore area, the number of osteoclasts and osteoblasts were lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f bone than Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone.
source: Both osteoclasts and osteoblasts were detected within the pores in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone, and due to the reduction in pore area, the number of osteoclasts and osteoblasts were lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f bone than Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by histomorphometry data shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: Voids in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone exhibited large highly active osteoclasts within the newly forming cortex.
source: When we assessed osteoclasts by TRAP staining, voids in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone exhibited large highly active osteoclasts within the newly forming cortex (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by TRAP staining shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: Resorption pits were observed in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f metaphyses.
source: Although murine osteoclasts do not usually demonstrate clear resorption pits, they were observed in this region in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f metaphyses (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 6J.

claim: The same region in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice rarely exhibited osteoclasts within the cortical pores.
source: In contrast to the increased resorption observed in the tibial cortex in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f metaphyses, the same region in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice rarely exhibited osteoclasts within the cortical pores (Figure 6H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figures 6H and 6I.

claim: The voids within the metaphyseal cortical bone of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice had greater osteoclast numbers than in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice, yet there was no difference in osteoblast numbers between the genotypes.
source: When quantified, the voids within the metaphyseal cortical bone of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice had greater osteoclast numbers than in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice, yet there was no difference in osteoblast numbers between the genotypes (Figure 6K,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by histomorphometry data shown in Figures 6K and 6L.

claim: Acp5 (the gene for TRAP) was significantly less in flushed femoral samples from Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: Analysis of flushed femoral samples, including mainly cortical bone provided some additional evidence of suppressed osteoclast formation in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice (Table 2); Acp5 (the gene for TRAP) was significantly less in these samples compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA data shown in Table 2.

claim: The reduction in Acp5 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice was not associated with a significant change in RANKL mRNA (Tnfsf11).
source: This was not associated with a significant change in RANKL mRNA (Tnfsf11), but OPG mRNA (Tnfrsf11b) levels were mildly, and barely statistically significantly, greater in samples from Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA data shown in Table 2.

claim: OPG mRNA (Tnfrsf11b) levels were mildly, and barely statistically significantly, greater in samples from Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: This was not associated with a significant change in RANKL mRNA (Tnfsf11), but OPG mRNA (Tnfrsf11b) levels were mildly, and barely statistically significantly, greater in samples from Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA data shown in Table 2.

claim: There was a greater proportion of marrow-filled area within the calvarial bone (diploe) in 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre mice.
source: To determine whether the cortical bone-specific effect on osteoclast formation could be detected at a second site, we carried out a preliminary analysis of calvarial bone from 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f and Dmp1Cre mice collected in our original study (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). There we observed a greater proportion of marrow-filled area within the calvarial bone (diploe) in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, and both a high level of calcein labelling, and abundant osteoclasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Calvarial bone from 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice showed both a high level of calcein labelling, and abundant osteoclasts.
source: To determine whether the cortical bone-specific effect on osteoclast formation could be detected at a second site, we carried out a preliminary analysis of calvarial bone from 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f and Dmp1Cre mice collected in our original study (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). There we observed a greater proportion of marrow-filled area within the calvarial bone (diploe) in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, and both a high level of calcein labelling, and abundant osteoclasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The stimulatory effect of SOCS3 deletion on bone resorption occurs also in calvarial cortical bone that has not formed through trabecular consolidation.
source: This confirms that the stimulatory effect of SOCS3 deletion on bone resorption occurs also in this cortical site that has not formed through trabecular consolidation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the calvarial bone observations.

claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited a more mature osteocyte canalicular network than Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: The higher level of resorption in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone was reflected in Ploton silver stains carried out at a slightly more distal location in the tibia. Indeed, in this more mature region, Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited a more mature osteocyte canalicular network than Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f (Figure 6M,N).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ploton silver staining shown in Figures 6M and 6N.

claim: The more mature osteocyte canalicular network in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice was indicated by a greater proportion of osteocyte cell bodies aligned parallel to the bone surface, and less cement lines within the cortex.
source: This was indicated by a greater proportion of osteocyte cell bodies aligned parallel to the bone surface, and less cement lines within the cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ploton silver staining shown in Figures 6M and 6N.

claim: The normalized structure in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice resembled the canalicular network of Dmp1Cre mice in the same region.
source: The normalized structure resembled the canalicular network of Dmp1Cre mice in the same region (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with Ploton silver staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Normalization of cortical bone structure and maturation was associated with a significant reduction in phospho-STAT3 staining in osteocytes within the newly forming cortical bone.
source: This normalization of cortical bone structure and maturation was associated with a significant reduction in phospho-STAT3 staining in osteocytes within the newly forming cortical bone (Figure 6O–Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 6O–Q.

claim: For cortical consolidation to occur in the metaphysis, bone resorption must be suppressed, and this can be achieved by reducing gp130-dependent STAT3 phosphorylation in osteocytes.
source: This indicates that for cortical consolidation to occur in the metaphysis, bone resorption must be suppressed, and this can be achieved by reducing gp130-dependent STAT3 phosphorylation in osteocytes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing reduced resorption and normalized cortical structure in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.

claim: 26 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice had a 50% reduction in post-yield deformation compared to Dmp1Cre mice.
source: We previously reported lower mechanical strength of the femoral diaphysis of 26 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre mice (tested by three point bending) (Cho et al., 2017). This included a 50% reduction in post-yield deformation (Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claim: Post-yield deformation was approximately doubled in both male and female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: In the present study, when Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice were crossed with Il6stf/f mice, this parameter was approximately doubled in both male and female mice (Table 3), representing a significant improvement.
evidence: This claim is supported by mechanical testing data shown in Table 3.

claim: Male Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited a significant reduction in yield force compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: Male mice Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice also exhibited a significant reduction in yield force.
evidence: This claim is supported by mechanical testing data shown in Table 3.

claim: The bone of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice is more ductile.
source: This suggests that the bone of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice is more ductile.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the mechanical testing data.

claim: Post-yield strain was significantly greater in both male and female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to the mutant Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
source: In addition, post-yield strain (which corrects the mechanical testing data for the size and shape of each individual bone sample) was significantly greater in both male and female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to the mutant Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (Table 3).

claim: The rescue of the strength defect in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice resulted from an improvement in the material quality of the cortical bone at the diaphysis, consistent with an improvement in cortical bone maturation.
source: This suggests that the rescue of the strength defect in these mice resulted from an improvement in the material quality of the cortical bone at the diaphysis, consistent with an improvement in cortical bone maturation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the mechanical testing data.

claim: Cortical bone formation includes both consolidation of structural elements and a transition from less organised and less mineralized bone to a mature lamellar structure.
source: This study shows that cortical bone formation includes both consolidation of structural elements and a transition from less organised and less mineralized bone to a mature lamellar structure; new methods were developed to show this.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data showing both morphological changes and density changes during cortical maturation.

claim: Consolidation, maturation, and mechanical performance of the cortical structure requires suppression of STAT3 phosphorylation downstream of gp130 signalling in osteocytes.
source: In addition, we show that consolidation, maturation, and mechanical performance of the cortical structure requires suppression of STAT3 phosphorylation downstream of gp130 signalling in osteocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the rescue of the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype by gp130 deletion.

claim: When STAT3 phosphorylation is elevated, osteoclasts actively resorb the cortical structure, and formation of a lamellar structure is delayed.
source: When STAT3 phosphorylation is elevated, osteoclasts actively resorb the cortical structure, and formation of a lamellar structure is delayed.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data showing increased osteoclasts and delayed lamellar bone formation in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.

claim: The transformation from a foamy woven bone cortex to a continuous cortical mass normally occurs between 10 and 14 days of age in C57BL/6 mice.
source: Normally the transformation from a foamy woven bone cortex to a continuous cortical mass occurs between 10 and 14 days of age in C57BL/6 mice (Bortel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bortel et al., 2015.

claim: The transformation from a foamy woven bone cortex to a continuous cortical mass coincides with rapid longitudinal growth, and occurs prior to development of the femoral elliptical shape.
source: This coincides with rapid longitudinal growth, and occurs prior to development of the femoral elliptical shape.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about bone development.

claim: Cortical consolidation in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice occurred after both bone length and femoral shape are established.
source: Since cortical consolidation in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice occurred after both bone length and femoral shape are established (Cho et al., 2017), we reasoned that their metaphyses could be used to track cortical consolidation without the complication of coincident changes in bone size and shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claim: New bone deposited at the growth plate is progressively replaced with bone of higher mineral density as the bone ages.
source: Closure of pores and increased mineralisation were both delayed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, consistent with very early work showing that new bone deposited at the growth plate is progressively replaced with bone of higher mineral density as the bone ages (Enlow, 1962), and more recent work showing that adolescent bone has higher mineral content than infant bone (Zimmermann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Enlow, 1962.

claim: Adolescent bone has higher mineral content than infant bone.
source: Closure of pores and increased mineralisation were both delayed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, consistent with very early work showing that new bone deposited at the growth plate is progressively replaced with bone of higher mineral density as the bone ages (Enlow, 1962), and more recent work showing that adolescent bone has higher mineral content than infant bone (Zimmermann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zimmermann et al., 2019.

claim: Delayed cortical development in childhood could lead to compromised bone strength later in life.
source: Clearly in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, this process is slowed, a defect that may explain the reduced ductility of bone in the presence of normal bone mass in the 6 month old female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (Cho et al., 2017). This raised the question of whether delayed cortical development in childhood could lead to compromised bone strength later in life.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the implications of the findings in the mouse model for human health.

claim: Measurement of cortical porosity is a technique now common in micro-computed tomography studies of murine bone.
source: Measurement of cortical porosity is a technique now common in micro-computed tomography studies of murine bone, but in this case, measuring the cortical pores in the metaphysis was challenging due to the difficulty of defining cortical and trabecular bone compartments.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about micro-CT methods.

claim: At the resolution of a standard micro-CT instrument, the pores measured are significantly larger than osteocyte lacunae.
source: At the resolution of a standard micro-CT instrument, the pores measured by this technique are significantly larger than osteocyte lacunae, and the majority of these pores are 'open pores' that connect with other pores, and with the top or bottom of the measurement region.
evidence: This claim is based on technical knowledge about micro-CT resolution.

evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: The pores in 12 week old female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f samples are large enough to contain blood vessels, osteoclasts, osteoblasts, and bone marrow.
source: This indicates they are large enough to contain blood vessels, osteoclasts, osteoblasts, and bone marrow, and similar to the pores detected histologically in Figure 6F and G.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the measured pore size and comparison with histological observations.

claim: It is often surmised that rodent bone does not remodel after the cortical shape has been established.
source: We were surprised to observe a significant transformation from mid- to high-density bone in control mice between 12 and 15 weeks, after the cortical bone had formed. It is often surmised that rodent bone does not remodel after the cortical shape has been established.
evidence: This claim represents a common assumption in the field.

claim: Resorption cavities have only been described in murine bone after 52 weeks of age.
source: However, although resorption cavities have only been described in murine bone after 52 weeks of age, lamellar bone content in bone increases even between 22 and 91 weeks of age; this occurs through an asymmetrical process where woven bone on the periosteum or the endocortical surface is resorbed and replaced by lamellar bone (Ferguson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferguson et al., 2003.

claim: Lamellar bone content in bone increases even between 22 and 91 weeks of age in mice; this occurs through an asymmetrical process where woven bone on the periosteum or the endocortical surface is resorbed and replaced by lamellar bone.
source: However, although resorption cavities have only been described in murine bone after 52 weeks of age, lamellar bone content in bone increases even between 22 and 91 weeks of age; this occurs through an asymmetrical process where woven bone on the periosteum or the endocortical surface is resorbed and replaced by lamellar bone (Ferguson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferguson et al., 2003.

claim: The increase in mineral content in control mice between 12 and 15 weeks may reflect secondary mineralization of the established bone matrix.
source: However, in the control mice, it is surprising that such a dramatic increase in the proportion of highly mineralized bone has occurred within a three week time period, suggesting that the increase in mineral content may also reflect secondary mineralization of the established bone matrix.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism of the observed density increase.

source: This provided a relatively simple way to measure the changes in bone maturation that occur with bone age in the same tissue samples, since the metaphysis contains both young and older bone.

evidence: This claim is based on speculation about potential applications of the method.

claim: The delayed metaphyseal development of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone indicates that cortical formation requires SOCS3 expression by Dmp1Cre positive cells (most likely late-stage osteoblasts and osteocytes).
source: The delayed metaphyseal development of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone indicates that cortical formation requires SOCS3 expression by Dmp1Cre positive cells (most likely late-stage ostoblasts and osteocytes).

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chia et al., 2015.

claim: Osteoblast lineage cells do not express erythropoietin receptor.
source: Although pharmacological treatment with erythropoietin modifies bone mass, and activates JAK/STAT signalling, we did not test the response to erythropoietin since in vivo lineage tracing studies have shown that osteoblast lineage cells do not express this receptor (Singbrant et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Singbrant et al., 2011.

claim: G-CSFR mRNA (Csf3r) is not found in cultured osteoblast lineage cells (primary osteoblasts, osteoblast cell lines, and the MLO-Y4 osteocyte-like cell line).
source: G-CSF did not induce a STAT3 phosphorylation response even in control animals, consistent with earlier studies reporting that G-CSFR mRNA (Csf3r) is not found in cultured osteoblast lineage cells (primary osteoblasts, osteoblast cell lines, and the MLO-Y4 osteocyte-like cell line) (Katayama et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Katayama et al., 2006.

claim: OSM and LIF have been shown previously to stimulate STAT3 phosphorylation in osteoblasts cultured to express osteocyte markers in vitro, and to suppress sclerostin expression in osteocytes in vitro and in vivo.
source: OSM and LIF have been shown previously to stimulate STAT3 phosphorylation in osteoblasts cultured to express osteocyte markers in vitro, and to suppress sclerostin expression in osteocytes in vitro and in vivo (Walker et al., 2010; Walker et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Walker et al., 2010 and Walker et al., 2016.

claim: IL-11 stimulates STAT3 phosphorylation in primary calvarial osteoblasts.
source: A response of osteocytes to IL-11 has not been reported previously, but IL-11 stimulates STAT3 phosphorylation in primary calvarial osteoblasts (Romas et al., 1996), and we have observed downregulation of sclerostin by IL-11 in an osteosarcoma-derived cell line (UMR106-01, Patricia W.M. Ho, unpublished data).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Romas et al., 1996.

source: A response of osteocytes to IL-11 has not been reported previously, but IL-11 stimulates STAT3 phosphorylation in primary calvarial osteoblasts (Romas et al., 1996), and we have observed downregulation of sclerostin by IL-11 in an osteosarcoma-derived cell line (UMR106-01, Patricia W.M. Ho, unpublished data).
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: At least three members of the IL-6 family (OSM, LIF, IL-11) may require suppression to enable cortical maturation.
source: In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone, STAT3 responses to these cytokines were elevated and prolonged in mice lacking SOCS3. This indicates that at least three members of this cytokine family may require suppression to enable cortical maturation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the STAT3 phosphorylation data.

claim: gp130 is a signalling receptor for a wide range of bone-active cytokines.
source: While we identified that gp130 is the receptor that must be suppressed for cortical consolidation, we did not identify a responsible hyperactive gp130-dependent cytokine. There are many candidates since gp130 is a signalling receptor for a wide range of bone-active cytokines (Sims, 2015; Sims, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sims, 2015 and Sims, 2016.

claim: IL-11, OSM and LIF are all required for normal osteoclast formation.
source: Our western blot data suggest that IL-11, OSM and LIF are all candidates. All three showed extended STAT3 phosphorylation in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, and all three are required for normal osteoclast formation (Sims et al., 2005; Walker et al., 2010; Poulton et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sims et al., 2005, Walker et al., 2010, and Poulton et al., 2012.

claim: Cardiotrophin-1 may be involved in cortical consolidation since it modifies osteoclast formation and activity in vivo, and acts directly on osteocytes to reduce sclerostin expression.

evidence: This claim is based on speculation supported by citations to Walker et al., 2008 and Walker et al., 2010.

source: We suggest that IL-11, OSM, and LIF at least must be suppressed in osteocytes to limit their production of factors, such as RANKL, that promote osteoclastogenesis in the developing cortical region, thereby allowing bone formation to dominate and consolidate the cortical structure.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing the role of gp130 signaling in cortical consolidation.
